Idioms.phrase: To follow up on something - To check up on someone or something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Nicole told me that she went to an interview a few days ago. She thinks she did really well on it and that she has a good chance of getting the job. She is wondering, though, whether or not she should follow up on it by sending a polite email.

Idioms.phrase: To get bent out of shape - To become upset.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't get cry about it! There's really no reason to get so bent out of shape over a simple disagreement.

Idioms.phrase: To get in touch with - To contact.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It's strange that they haven't heard from Patricia this week. She promised that she'd get in touch with them.

Idioms.phrase: To get rid of - To do away with something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think I'll get rid of all those old video tapes. After all, there's not much I can do with them now.

Idioms.phrase: To get your walking papers - To get fired from your job.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I have terrible news. Darren got his walking papers today. He's going to have to look for a new job.

Idioms.phrase: To give in - To decide to go along with something, usually as a result of some sort of pressure.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Their parents eventually gave in and said that they were allowed to go on a summer vacation with their friends.

Idioms.phrase: To give someone the heads-up - To notify someone of something and to keep them up-to-date.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Beth sent an email to all of her friends, detailing her events for the big event. They really appreciated her giving them the heads-up.

Idioms.phrase: To go down like a lead balloon - To be terribly received by an audience.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The new play did really badly. The audience hated it, and it went down like a lead balloon.

Idioms.phrase: To go Dutch - For every individual to pay for their own bill in a restaurant.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We decided to go Dutch at dinner. After all, it's so much easier when each person just pays for what they've eaten.

Idioms.phrase: To go for broke - To gamble all of your resources.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Maggie decided to go for broke with her new endeavor. She has almost no money left. I hope it works out for her, but it seems pretty risky!

Idioms.phrase: To go off the deep end - To get extremely upset and/or emotional.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Linda went off the deep end when she heard the bad news. I don't think I've ever seen anyone so upset.

Idioms.phrase: To have another thing coming - To have something else that will happen in the near future that you didn't expect or think would happen.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Melinda thinks that her plan will work, but I say that she has another thing coming.

Idioms.phrase: To have one's back to the wall - To feel trapped, with no real options to deal with the situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jayden felt that his back was to the wall. He couldn't figure out how to get out of the situation; he didn't feel like he had any options to deal with it either.

Idioms.phrase: To hold out an olive branch - To offer a gesture of peace or to ask for forgiveness or a truce.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Judy and Adelaide had been friends for years but they didn't speak for a few months after they had an argument. Finally, Adelaide decided to hold out an olive branch.

Idioms.phrase: To hold your own - To be confident and politely assertive with other people and in various situations.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about my sister. She can hold her own in any situation. It's because she's so confident.

Idioms.phrase: To keep an eye on - To closely watch and/or monitor.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Thomas is a very careful investor. He's always keeping an eye on the stock market.

Idioms.phrase: To know by sight - To know someone when you look at them.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Dan couldn't remember her face, but he knew her on sight.

Idioms.phrase: To live beyond your means - To live in a manner that requires more money than you can afford.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I told them that it's very unwise to live beyond one's means. It can lead you into a lot of debt.

Idioms.phrase: To live hand-to-mouth - To live with very little money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They lived pretty much hand-to-mouth after they both lost their jobs.

Idioms.phrase: To look down one's nose - To feel superior to someone else.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Juliana always looked down her nose at me and my friends. She was quite conceited and always thought she was above us.

Idioms.phrase: To make a long story short - To tell someone something in a brief and simple way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Lots of things happened yesterday. To make a long story short, we had a terrible time.

Idioms.phrase: To make a mountain out of a molehill - To overreact and overstate a situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You're blowing this out of proportion! Stop making a mountain out of a molehill. It's really not a very serious situation.

Idioms.phrase: To make matters worse - To worsen a problem.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We were late for the party. And to make matters worse, we couldn’t find a parking space.

Idioms.phrase: To nix something - To cancel a plan or dismiss an idea, or to forbid something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She decided to nix their plans to go away this winter. It was no longer possible.

Idioms.phrase: To outdo oneself - To do better at something that one has done before.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Sophie was proud of herself last week. She outdid her previous achievements at the gym.

Idioms.phrase: To paddle your own canoe - To be self-sufficient and think independently.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Josh has always been one to paddle his own canoe. He's very independent and does what he thinks is best, without seeking help from others.

Idioms.phrase: To pony up - To pay money that is owed or that you need to pay for some other reason.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Come on and pony up! You know you still owe me that ten dollars I lent you a month ago.

Idioms.phrase: To run/blow hot and cold - To sometimes seem enthusiastic and other times seem the opposite.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was worried that his girlfriend didn't like him anymore. She seemed to blow hot and cold. Sometimes she seemed to like him a lot, while other times she didn't.

Idioms.phrase: To see the light - To finally see something clearly and understand it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was so happy to hear that Victoria had seen the light about her boyfriend. He isn't very nice and she finally realizes that now.

Idioms.phrase: To serve one right - It was a just consequence or punishment.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It serves him right! He did some really careless things; he deserves to suffer the consequences.

Idioms.phrase: To smooth things over - To restore peace to a situation or to resolve conflict.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Denise was good at helping her friends resolve arguments. She liked to help smooth things over.

Idioms.phrase: To stand up for - To help defend someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jill always stood up for me when others tried to bully me at school.

Idioms.phrase: To start over from scratch - To start over again from the very beginning.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The birthday cake I made yesterday was a total disaster. I had to start over from scratch.

Idioms.phrase: To stonewall - To be intentionally vague or to make insignificant statements in response to a question, specifically to avoid answering it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They tried to ask him questions but he was always stonewalling, finding ways to avoid giving real answers.

Idioms.phrase: To take a load off someone's back - To relieve someone of a specific burden or a potential burden.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My friends really showed they cared when they took that load off my back. I would have had a terrible time without their help.

Idioms.phrase: To take it easy - To relax and/or rest.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Belle just finished a busy week at school. She's looking forward to taking it easy this weekend.

Idioms.phrase: To take something for granted - To assume that you would have had, or will have, something no matter what.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, People accused Adrian of taking his friends for granted. He always just assumed that they'd be there for him, without giving them any consideration.

Idioms.phrase: To the hilt - To do something in an extremely thorough way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They went shopping for new summer wardrobes yesterday. They did it to the hilt, I have to say.

Idioms.phrase: Tongue-in-cheek - In a humorous spirit.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I couldn't figure out why she took what I said seriously. It was obvious that I meant it in a tongue-in-cheek way; I even laughed afterward.

Idioms.phrase: Too big for one's boots - Conceited and arrogant.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't you agree that Ben is too big for his boots? I think he is. He's very conceited.

Idioms.phrase: Too many irons in the fire - To have an excessive number of activities taking up your time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She was having a hard time concentrating on her work. After speaking to her, I realized that she has too many irons in the fire. Having so many things to worry about makes it hard to focus.

Idioms.phrase: Top dog - The person in charge.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Our boss is the top dog in this office.

Idioms.phrase: Top-notch - Top quality.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The perfume he bought me for my birthday is top-notch. It’s a designer brand and extremely expensive. I love it.

Idioms.phrase: Touch and go - An uncertain or otherwise precarious situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The situation was touch and go for a while. We had no way of knowing what would happen. Would everything be okay in the end?

Idioms.phrase: Touch base - To get in contact with someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Could you please touch base with me next week, to let me know how the project is progressing?

Idioms.phrase: Track record - A history of doing something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He has an excellent track record when it comes to academics. Have you seen his grades? They're great!

Idioms.phrase: Train of thought - Ideas that come one after the other and are connected.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The alarm interrupted my train of thought. Now I can't remember what I had decided about the presentation.

Idioms.phrase: Train wreck - Someone who has a chaotic and probably unsuccessful life.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She was upset when her old friend called her a train wreck.

Idioms.phrase: Travel light - To travel with very little luggage.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They decided to travel light for their trip to Europe, as they planned to do some backpacking.

Idioms.phrase: Treat someone to something - To buy something for someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They treated the kids to ice cream yesterday.

Idioms.phrase: Treat/handle someone with kid gloves - To treat someone or something with extreme gentleness and respect.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They realized that, since their boss was so sensitive about his ideas, they would need to treat his pet project with kid gloves.

Idioms.phrase: Troubled waters - A difficult and unstable situation, and/or emotionally difficult times.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My friend helped me overcome troubled waters last year. I was scared because my situation at home seemed too unsettled and precarious.

Idioms.phrase: True blue - Loyal and trustworthy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Amy was true blue as a friend. I could always count on her to be there for me.

Idioms.phrase: Tuckered out - Very tired.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I had thought about going out tonight after work, but I'm just too tuckered out.

Idioms.phrase: Turn a blind eye - To refuse to acknowledge the reality of something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We couldn't get Tommy to believe us about what had happened. He just wanted to turn a blind eye to it.

Idioms.phrase: Turn a place upside down - To search for something, probably an item one has lost, in a frantic way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I couldn't find it, even though I turned my living room upside down while searching for it.

Idioms.phrase: Turn over a new leaf - To change your life in order to make it (and probably your behavior) better.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Sarah said that she was going to turn over a new leaf in her life. She had made some bad decisions in the past, but she was determined to make better ones in the future.

Idioms.phrase: Turn the other cheek - To refrain from retaliating against something that offends you.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Olivia was always so patient and forgiving with everyone. If anyone did something that upset her, she would often turn the other cheek.

Idioms.phrase: Turn the tables - To switch places someone, putting them in the same sort of position you once occupied.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He turned the tables on the bully by standing up for himself; he showed everyone that the bully was really the one people should ignore.

Idioms.phrase: Turn up the heat - To increase the amount of pressure on a person or situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The lawyer turned up the heat in his questioning of the witness.

Idioms.phrase: Twist someone's arm - To try to coerce someone into doing something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Sally didn't want to go to the amusement park at first, but her friends twisted her arm.

Idioms.phrase: Two peas in a pod - Extremely similar and probably close.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The little girl and her best friend were very much alike. They were like two peas in a pod.

Idioms.phrase: Under a cloud - Being under some kind of suspicion.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Mike said that people thought he had done something wrong even though he hadn't. He found it hard to interact with them under that cloud.

Idioms.phrase: Under someone's thumb - To be under the control of someone else.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jesse was under Alex's thumb. He looked up to Alex and wanted to be like him, but this ended up meaning that his friend could control him.

Idioms.phrase: Under the table/counter - Illegally or secretly (especially with regard to being paid in such a way).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They received payments under the table. They didn't want to claim the money on their income taxes.

Idioms.phrase: Under the weather - Not feeling well.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Kristen wanted to come with us to the party, but she's feeling really under the weather. We think she might have flu.

Idioms.phrase: Under the wire - To finish something just before it has to be completed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Abby will probably get her paper done right under the wire. You know what she's like! She left it to the last minute.

Idioms.phrase: Until the cows come home - A very long time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think they'll be arguing about this until the cows come home! I can't see them ever stopping.

Idioms.phrase: Up a blind alley - Taking a course of action that will lead to a negative outcome.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I tried to convince him that he was going up a blind alley with his new plan, but he wouldn't believe me. I think things will turn out badly.

Idioms.phrase: Up a gum tree - In a very difficult situation that might be impossible to extricate oneself from.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I've been looking at the situation and, honestly, I think we're up a gum tree. I don't know how we can get ourselves out of this.

Idioms.phrase: Up for grabs - Available to obtain.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, There is a lot of money up for grabs in the raffle. Let's hope we win!

Idioms.phrase: Up in arms - To be very upset or angry about something specific.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The protestors were up in arms about the new law. They thought it was oppressive and wanted it to be changed.

Idioms.phrase: Up in the air - Not yet decided.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Plans for our vacation this year are pretty much up in the air. There are so many options and we just can't decide among them.

Idioms.phrase: Up the creek without a paddle - To be in a bad situation and not be able to find a way to solve it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Maisie doesn't know what to do about the situation. She feels like she's up the creek without a paddle.

Idioms.phrase: Up to snuff - Meeting the standard of quality required.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My brother got a disappointing grade on his essay. The teacher said it just wasn't up to snuff.

Idioms.phrase: Upset the apple cart - To disturb the current situation or status quo in some way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The employees didn't like the new changes their boss had made to their terms of employment, so they all decided to upset the apple cart and object.

Idioms.phrase: Use your loaf - Use your brain and think.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, How could you not realize that you would need to do that? It's common sense. You really need to use your loaf!

Idioms.phrase: Veg out - To relax and not think about anything that stresses you out.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Let's not do much this afternoon. We can just veg out and enjoy some television.

Idioms.phrase: Walk in someone's shoes - To imagine yourself in someone else's position.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Janet was a very empathetic person. She always tried to imagine herself in the other person's shoes before making any sort of judgment or offering advice.

Idioms.phrase: Walk in the park - An easy and pleasant time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The new job was certainly no walk in the park. It was quite challenging and difficult.

Idioms.phrase: Walking on air - Happy or joyous.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Laura called me to say how happy she is about the prize she won. She seems to be walking on air.

Idioms.phrase: Wallflower - Someone (usually a girl or woman) who is shy and doesn’t receive any attention, especially at a dance.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Marjorie was sad that she was always such a wallflower at dances. No one ever asked her to dance. Marie, on the other hand, was the opposite of a wallflower. She was very popular and everyone wanted to talk to her.

Idioms.phrase: Washing my hands of something/someone - To completely stop caring about, and dealing with, someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I wanted to convince her that we could be friends. She has kept on being rude though, so I think I'll need to wash my hands of her.

Idioms.phrase: Waste not, want not - If you refrain from wasting things, you won't have to go without.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Their grandmother was very good at saving and reusing things. Waste not, want not was her motto.

Idioms.phrase: Watch out for - To keep alert and look around for something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Watch out for bugs when you go for your hike next week.

Idioms.phrase: Water under the bridge - Something that is now in the past and that isn't important anymore.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I can't understand why Melissa is still so worried about what happened. It really wasn't very important, and now it’s water under the bridge. It's in the past.

Idioms.phrase: Watering hole - A bar (where alcohol is served).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My friends headed to a local watering hole for a few drinks.

Idioms.phrase: Wave of the future - Something that will be extremely prevalent in the future.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The company said that the new technology they invested in is sure to be the wave of the future.

Idioms.phrase: We see eye to eye - We see things the same way and agree.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Many of her friends had disagreed with her on the issue, so she was glad to find that I agreed with her; we see eye to eye on other topics as well.

Idioms.phrase: Wear many different hats - To have several different distinct roles.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Lindsay wears many different hats at her company. She works in at least three departments.

Idioms.phrase: Wear your heart on your sleeve - To let your emotions be very obvious.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Chelsea is always very open about things. She really wears her heart on her sleeve; you can always tell what kind of mood she’s in.

Idioms.phrase: Weasel out of something - To get out of doing something or taking responsibility for something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jane managed to weasel out of having to take her little brother to her appointment yesterday.

Idioms.phrase: Weather the storm - Successfully come through some sort of difficulty.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, There were lots of problems that we had to deal with and some people were afraid that they could not endure it. I was sure that we would weather the storm, though.

Idioms.phrase: Well begun is half done - It's important to get a good start.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Megan was worried that she wouldn't do a good job on the project, but I thought she'd made a really good start. I reassured her and reminded her that well begun is half done.

Idioms.phrase: We'll cross that bridge when we come to it - We will deal with that problem when we have to.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about that problem right now. We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

Idioms.phrase: Well-heeled - Wealthy and well-dressed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Chloe started working at an upscale boutique this week. She told me a bit about all of her well-heeled customers.

Idioms.phrase: Went the extra mile - To do even more than is required.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The group went the extra mile with their class project. They did more than was required and ended up with an A+.

Idioms.phrase: Wet behind the ears - Inexperienced and probably young.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The new guy in the office is really young and wet behind the ears. He hardly has any experience in this field.

Idioms.phrase: Wet blanket - An individual who others feel ruins a fun or enjoyable experience.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Dan is such a wet blanket. He always tries to ruin the fun when we're having a party.

Idioms.phrase: Wet my whistle - Have a drink of something when thirsty.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Could you hold on a second? I need a few sips of water, just to wet my whistle.

Idioms.phrase: What are you up to? - What are you doing? (Often there is an implication the person in question is doing something they shouldn't; this can be playful in meaning.)
Idioms.definition: As in this example, What are you up to? Are you eating candy even though lunch is in an hour?
